subject: ela
intro: Many stories, especially fables, folktales, and myths, teach a lesson. The central message is the big idea the author wants you to remember, like "be kind" or "don't give up." You find it by asking what a character learns or how a character changes by the end, then pointing to the key details that show it. State the lesson in your own words and back it up with the story.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

A thirsty crow found a pitcher with a little water at the bottom, too low to reach. One by one, the crow dropped pebbles into the pitcher until the water rose to the top. Then the crow drank.

What is the lesson of this fable?

steps: Ask what the crow does to solve its problem.
The crow could not reach the water, so it "dropped pebbles" until the water rose.
The crow used a smart idea instead of giving up.
solution.answer: The lesson is that clever thinking can solve a hard problem. The crow raised the water by dropping in pebbles instead of giving up.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

An ant worked all summer storing food, while a grasshopper played and stored nothing. When winter came, the grasshopper was hungry and cold, but the ant had plenty.

What lesson does this fable teach?

steps: Compare what each character does and how it ends.
The ant "worked all summer" and had food; the grasshopper "played" and went hungry.
Planning ahead paid off for the ant.
solution.answer: The lesson is to plan and work ahead for the future. The ant prepared all summer and had food, while the grasshopper, who only played, went hungry.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Lina bragged that she was the fastest runner and never practiced. Quiet Sara practiced every day. At the race, Sara passed Lina at the finish line.

What is the central message?

steps: Notice who brags and who works, and who wins.
Lina "bragged" and "never practiced"; Sara "practiced every day" and won.
Steady effort beat bragging.
solution.answer: The message is that steady practice matters more than bragging. Sara, who practiced every day, won the race, while Lina only boasted.

items.prompt:
Read the folktale.

A lion caught a tiny mouse but let it go. Later, the lion was trapped in a hunter's net. The little mouse chewed through the ropes and set the lion free.

What lesson does the folktale teach?

steps: Notice how the small mouse repays the lion.
The lion showed mercy, and later "the little mouse chewed through the ropes."
Even a small friend can help you.
solution.answer: The lesson is that even a small or weak friend can be a big help, so it pays to be kind to everyone. The tiny mouse rescued the mighty lion.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

Each day a boy shouted "Wolf!" as a joke, and the villagers ran to help, finding nothing. When a real wolf came and the boy shouted, no one came.

What is the lesson of this fable?

steps: Notice what happens after the boy lies again and again.
He cried "Wolf!" as a joke, so when it was real, "no one came."
Lying made people stop believing him.
solution.answer: The lesson is that people stop believing a liar, even when they finally tell the truth. Because the boy lied for fun, no one helped him when the wolf was real.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

No one on the block would talk to grumpy Mr. Ito. But when young Kai kept saying good morning every day, Mr. Ito slowly started to smile and wave back.

What central message does this story share?

steps: Notice what Kai keeps doing and how Mr. Ito changes.
Kai "kept saying good morning every day," and grumpy Mr. Ito "started to smile and wave back."
Steady kindness warmed him up.
solution.answer: The message is that steady kindness can win people over. Kai's daily greetings turned grumpy Mr. Ito friendly.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

A fox tried again and again to reach some grapes but could not jump high enough. At last it walked away, muttering, "Those grapes are probably sour anyway."

What does this fable teach about people?

steps: Notice what the fox says after it fails.
The fox could not reach the grapes, then called them "probably sour anyway."
It pretended not to want what it could not get.
solution.answer: The fable teaches that people sometimes pretend not to want what they cannot have. The fox called the grapes sour only because it failed to reach them.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Two goats met on a narrow bridge, each refusing to step back. They pushed and pushed until both tumbled into the river below.

What lesson can readers learn from the goats?

steps: Notice why both goats end up in the river.
Each goat "refused to step back," so "both tumbled into the river."
Neither would give a little, so both lost.
solution.answer: The lesson is that stubbornness can hurt everyone; sometimes you must give a little to avoid losing a lot. Because neither goat backed up, both fell in the river.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Dev planned to build the whole model rocket in one night and rushed every step. Pieces fell off and paint smeared. His sister took a week, one careful step at a time, and hers stood perfect.

What is the central message, and which detail shows it best?

steps: Compare Dev's rushing with his sister's care.
Dev "rushed every step" and pieces "fell off"; his sister worked "one careful step at a time" and hers "stood perfect."
Taking your time led to a better result.
solution.answer: The message is that careful, patient work beats rushing. The detail that shows it best is that Dev's rushed rocket fell apart while his sister's careful one "stood perfect."

items.prompt:
Read the story.

When the class garden failed, everyone blamed each other until Priya said, "Let's just each water one row." They split the work, and by spring the garden bloomed.

State the lesson of this story in your own words and name a detail that supports it.

steps: Notice what changes once they stop blaming and start sharing the work.
Priya suggests, "Let's just each water one row," and the garden "bloomed."
Working together fixed the problem.
solution.answer: Lesson: working together solves problems better than blaming each other. Supporting detail: once they "split the work," the garden "bloomed."
